content: We will assess agent evaluation design. You have an agent that sometimes chooses the wrong tool but still produces a plausible final answer. What layers of evaluation would you build, and which failures cannot be caught by final-answer matching alone?

I would have unit tests for deterministic tools and maybe golden answers for common scenarios. If the final answer looks right I might still miss that it chose a dangerous tool or wrote bad memory, so I need trajectory assertions too, but I have not designed those deeply.
Suppose the same model generates the answer and grades its own answer. Why can the eval report look stable while the system is still wrong? Give a concrete mitigation.

The model can share the same blind spot as its own answer, so it can consistently approve the same mistake. I would use a different judge or deterministic rules for things that can be expressed as invariants.
Last probe: your agent has persistent memory and behaves correctly for one session but degrades after 50 interactions. How would you construct a test that catches that?
I would replay a long sequence and compare state after checkpoints, especially whether old memory leaks into current decisions. I am less sure how to make the semantic parts stable across models.
I have enough diagnostic signal and will end the assessment without teaching.
